summary: Redwood AE + SE walked Harbor Dataworks through org-level and project-level API keys, fair-share rate limiting, concurrent request caps, and quota enforcement patterns. Discussion focused on how to map Harbor's teams to org/project keys, billing per-project, burst handling, and policy rollout strategies. Action items: pricing worksheet, policy examples, sample logs for a POC.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-05-14 16:00 PDT | Duration: 52 minutes | Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Jared Cole (CTO Harbor), Lina Gomez (Platform Eng), Marcus Reed (SRE)

[00:00] Ethan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Ethan Park, account exec on the infra team, Priya is our solutions engineer. How's the timing for an hour?
[00:08] Jared (CTO): Works for us, we blocked 60 just in case.
[00:11] Priya (SE): Great. Agenda — we'll run a short demo in the Console showing org vs project key behavior, then deep-dive into rate limits: fair-share, burst, concurrency, and then Q&A and next steps.
[00:25] Lina: Sounds good. We're especially interested in how we can give product teams their own keys and still keep global guardrails. Also billing per-project is a must.
[00:33] Ethan: Perfect, that's what we'll target.

[00:40] Priya: I'm going to share my screen — pulling up the Console. Apologies, the recording indicator might show a little late. First slide: high-level concepts. Org key is the top-level identity; project keys sit under orgs and can have specific quotas and routing rules.
[01:05] Priya: Example: org key for Harbor defaults to 1m tokens/day; we can carve out 200k tokens for product-a project key and 50k for internal tooling project key. Fair-share comes into play when multiple projects hit the same org pool.
[01:28] Marcus (SRE): How are bursts handled? If product-a has a sudden spike, can it borrow from the org pool?
[01:35] Priya: Yes, we support burst buckets and configurable burst policies. You can set a per-project burst allowance plus an org-level overprovisioning buffer. When a project uses its burst, it first consumes its project bucket, then if allowed, consumes from the org buffer until the org quota is reached.
[01:55] (transcription note: 'burst' got transcribed as 'birst' once)

[02:05] Ethan: A common pattern is weighted fair-share; if product-a is high priority, you can give it weight 5 and product-b weight 1. When contention happens, tokens are divided proportionally by weight.
[02:22] Jared: And does that affect latency? If a project is throttled, do requests get queued at runtime or fail fast?
[02:31] Priya: You can choose policies: fail-fast with 429, or queue with short backoffs up to a concurrency cap. For very latency-sensitive routes, we recommend fail-fast and a dedicated capacity reservation (Redwood Dedicated) to avoid noisy neighbors.

[02:50] Lina: This is the part I wanted to ask about. We have a strict SLO on inference latency for the customer-facing product. Can we tie a project key to Dedicated capacity?
[02:58] Priya: Yes, project keys can be pinned to deployment tiers. In the Console we have a routing policy that maps a project key to a pool: hosted, dedicated, or private V P C. Note: sometimes the transcript shows VPC as V P C — audio misparse.

[03:22] Marcus: On security, we'll need SSO and SAML — sorry, 'Samuel' popped in the transcript — SAML for access. Also KMS for keys.
[03:31] Ethan: We integrate with SAML/SSO and support KMS/HSM for model keys and customer encryption. We'll attach our SOC 2 plus the security pack in the follow-up.

[03:44] Priya: Back to rate limits — open the policy editor. Quick note: the Console shows sample policy rules as JSON. I'll paste a short snippet — transcription may mangle braces but here it is as text: {
  "policy": "org-default",
  "rules": [
    {"scope":"project","rate_per_min":1000,"burst":200},
    {"scope":"org","rate_per_min":10000,"fair_share_weights":{"product-a":5,"product-b":1}}
  ]
}
(there's some mis-hearing of 'KV cache' as 'K V cash' earlier)

[04:35] Priya: You can define priority rules too, e.g., 'billing' routes have higher weight during business hours. We also support time-windowed quotas.
[04:50] Jared: If we set project keys for each team, can we charge back to individual teams? We need per-project usage reporting and invoice-level breakdown.
[04:59] Ethan: Yes, Console exposes token-level usage per project key, exportable as CSV or via the usage API. Many customers plug that into their internal chargeback tools.

[05:12] Priya: Now demo of sticky routing: if you want a request from product-a to always go to a particular model variant or region, you can set sticky attributes on the project key. That guarantees routing affinity unless the pool is degraded — then we fall back per the fallback policy.
[05:35] Marcus: What's the fallback behavior if dedicated pool is down?
[05:39] Priya: Automatic fallback to a compatible hosted model variant with degraded SLOs, and we emit trace events. You can also set automatic retries or failover to a lower-cost region.

[05:55] Ethan: Quick interjection — many teams prefer to have small canaries for new policies. The Console supports rollout percentages for new quota rules, so you can target 5% traffic, then ramp.
[06:10] Lina: Nice. Can we do canaries by header or by trace id?
[06:14] Priya: Yes, you can target by project key, header flag, or user id.

[06:22] (timestamp jump — demo continues, logs displayed)

[06:40] Priya: Now looking at Optimize: it surfaced suggestions for batching and prefix caching based on our sample logs. Optimize suggested increasing batch window from 8ms to 12ms for product-a which reduced per-token GPU cost by ~18% in our sim. It also flagged a heavy KV cache miss rate. Note: sometimes transcriber shows 'K V cache' as words.
[07:05] Marcus: We'll definitely want that — our request pattern has a lot of short chat completions. Is Optimize automated or manual recommendations?
[07:12] Priya: It's a recommendations engine. You can enable auto-applied suggestions in a sandbox mode; we won't change production policies without a manual opt-in.

[07:25] Jared: About quotas — do you support concurrency quotas per key, e.g., max 50 concurrent requests?
[07:31] Priya: Yes, concurrency quotas are supported. When concurrency is reached, options are: queue up to N requests with backoff, or return throughput-limited 429s. We also expose a real-time concurrency gauge in Console.

[07:50] Ethan: Also worth noting: rate limits can be soft or hard. Soft limits will degrade cost-first (raise latency) whereas hard limits will reject. Most customers use soft for internal teams and hard for external-facing product traffic.

[08:05] (brief cross talk, someone drops audio)

[08:20] Lina: Practical question: we have 12 teams and want to give each a project key. Do you recommend one org pool per business unit or a single org across all teams?
[08:31] Priya: It depends on trust boundaries. If you need strict separation for compliance, create multiple orgs. If you want centralized control and flexible redistribution, single org with project keys and weights is easier. We often see a hybrid: org per BU and project keys per product.

[08:52] Marcus: For billing, will usage from project keys show on the same invoice or per-org only?
[08:58] Ethan: Invoices are at the org level by default, but you can emit per-project usage exports. For true per-project invoicing, we have enterprise billing options to split invoices or integrate with your internal billing tool. We'll detail that in the worksheet.

[09:18] Priya: Let's flip to policy rollout demo — I'll create a new quota profile and show a canary to 10% of traffic. (typing) Creating rule... applied. The Console shows a live gauge: 2% currently. You can abort or ramp.
[09:43] Jared: Good. Can we version policies? We need audit logs.
[09:47] Priya: Yes, every policy change is versioned and we emit an audit event. We also provide a streamable audit log export for SIEM integration.

[10:02] Ethan: Security question; Harbors asked about data residency. Priya — pointer?
[10:07] Priya: We have region controls — you can pin models and keys to regions to keep inference in EU or US only. For on-prem or air-gapped, Redwood Private package is available. Again, audio sometimes shows 'Redwood Privatee' — transcriber glitch.

[10:22] Lina: About enforcement latency — when we change a policy, how quickly does it take effect?
[10:26] Priya: Policies are pushed to edge nodes within ~15-45s typically; there are caching windows but you can force an immediate rollout.

[10:36] Marcus: I want to drill into sticky routing and session affinity. If a user is mid conversation and the model variant is swapped, do you maintain the KV cache transfer?
[10:46] Priya: We do KV cache affinity for pinned sessions as long as the target model is compatible. If you fall back to a different variant, there is an option to warm the KV state or to accept cold start. We surface both behaviors in the trace.

[11:05] Ethan: I want to highlight a few edge cases we see: 1) Teams set project keys but keep root API keys in engineers' hands — we recommend disabling root keys and enforcing service accounts. 2) Beware of unlimited bursts if you don't set org buffer limits.

[11:28] Jared: Can we limit keys to only embedding or only generation?
[11:32] Priya: Yes, method-level restrictions exist. You can create a policy that prohibits embedding calls from specific keys.

[11:40] (transcription hiccup: 'embeddings' became 'embed dings' once)

[11:48] Ethan: Quick Q from my side — are there any regulatory constraints we should call out? GDPR and CCPA are common; we also support audit logs retention options for PCI-adjacent use cases.
[11:59] Lina: We'll need 12 months of logs and KMS integration. Also any SOC 2 in place?
[12:05] Ethan: Yes, SOC 2 Type II; we'll attach the report.

[12:12] (demo continues for next 25 minutes with specific Console clicks and live metrics; timestamps at roughly 15-60s intervals but trimmed here)

[35:10] Priya: Switching to a simulated load — I'm going to trigger concurrent requests as product-a and product-b and show the fair-share distribution. Watch the token burn rate and the per-project concurrency gauge.
[35:28] Marcus: I see product-a gets 5x tokens; product-b is limited per its weight. Good. The UI shows the 429s for product-b. Is there a programmatic hook so we can alert when a project hits 80% of its share?
[35:40] Priya: Yes, there are alert rules you can bind to usage thresholds and emit webhooks or integrate with PagerDuty.

[36:05] Jared: For the POC, we'd like to validate cost savings with Optimize suggestions. How intrusive are the batching changes to our code?
[36:14] Priya: Minimal — often just change to a batch endpoint with a slightly larger aggregation window. We can run a dry-run to show simulated savings before applying.

[36:30] Marcus: One more: can we limit concurrent embeddings separately from Chat?
[36:36] Priya: Yes, you can set method-specific concurrency and rate caps.

[36:45] Ethan: We're about to wrap. Any final questions?
[36:49] Lina: Two items — one, can you send the security pack and SOC? Two, we'll collect our traffic logs and send to Priya.
[36:57] Ethan: Absolutely. We'll also include the quota worksheet and sample policy.

[37:05] Priya: I'll drop the recording link and the sample policy JSON in the follow-up. Note again: some proper nouns in transcript may be off — 'Redwood Dedicated' turned into 'Redwood Dedicatede' earlier, and 'KV cache' as 'K V cash' — ignore those.

[37:22] Ethan: Recap: Ethan sends pricing/worksheet; Priya sends policy example and recording; Harbor shares logs; follow-up POC kickoff.
[37:32] Jared: Perfect. Thanks all.
[37:35] (meeting ends, informal chat for 2 minutes)

Post-meeting notes: demo included a live simulated load showing fair-share enforcement, canary policy rollout, region pinning, and Optimize recommendations. Customer expressed interest in a 2-week POC focusing on cost savings from batching and verifying latency SLOs under Dedicated vs hosted.

References / links mentioned: Console demo recording (link to be sent), Security pack (SOC2 report link), Quota worksheet (spreadsheet link).
